title: Constipation: first-line treatment
summary: First-line management of constipation in adults using osmotic and stool-softening agents.
changeSummary: Initial version based on NICE NG114 constipation guidance.
clinicalNotes: Constipation is common and often managed in primary care. Reassure patients that most cases resolve with lifestyle measures and laxatives.
Assess for red-flag symptoms requiring referral: weight loss, anaemia, change in bowel habit >2 weeks in adults >40 years, abdominal/rectal masses, new onset in >60 years.
Assess for medication-related causes: opioids (most common in healthcare settings), anticholinergics, iron supplements, calcium channel blockers. Consider de-prescribing if appropriate.

Lifestyle measures first: increase dietary fibre gradually (20-30g daily), increase fluid intake to 6-8 glasses daily, increase physical activity, respond to urge to defaecate without delay, avoid suppressing bowel urges.
Start bulk-forming laxatives (high-fibre diet) or osmotic laxatives for first-line treatment. Do not use stimulant laxatives routinely as first-line except in opioid-induced constipation.
If inadequate response after 2-4 weeks, add or switch to alternative laxative. Consider combination therapy (e.g. osmotic + stool softener).
Avoid prolonged use of stimulant laxatives as routine treatment due to risk of dependence and impaired colonic motor function.
Counsel on expected timescale: osmotic laxatives take 2-3 days; bulk-forming take several days. Manage expectations and avoid escalation too quickly.
Refer to secondary care if no response to treatment after 2-4 weeks, red-flag symptoms, or suspected organic cause.
cautions: Avoid high-fibre intake acutely if faecal impaction is suspected; risk of bowel obstruction.
Stimulant laxatives can cause abdominal cramping and should be used cautiously in functional bowel disorders.
Osmotic laxatives can cause bloating and flatulence; start low and titrate up gradually.
Warn about dehydration risk if inadequate fluid intake with osmotic or bulk-forming agents.
Avoid laxatives in acute abdominal pain, undiagnosed abdominal symptoms, or suspected bowel obstruction.

regimens.label: 1st choice: Osmotic laxative

components.dose: 15-30 mL once daily, increased to BD if needed
components.frequency: once daily initially, up to twice daily
components.duration: review after 2-4 weeks; can be long-term if effective

restrictions: Use with caution in diabetes (contains lactose-derived galactose).
notes: Gentle, takes 2-3 days to work.
May cause bloating and flatulence initially; reassure patient this often settles.
Increase fibre and fluid intake concurrently for best effect.

regimens.label: 1st choice: Alternative osmotic laxative — polyethylene glycol (macrogol)

components.duration: review after 2-4 weeks; can be long-term if effective

notes: Osmotic action; produces soft stools without stimulating peristalsis.
Generally well-tolerated; lower bloating risk than lactulose.
Effect may be seen within 24-48 hours but can take up to 72 hours.
Mix with water (typically 125 mL per sachet); can add to drinks for palatability.

regimens.label: 1st choice: Bulk-forming laxative (if patient prefers)

components.dose: 1 sachet or 2 teaspoons twice daily (morning and evening)
components.duration: can be used long-term as dietary fibre supplement

restrictions: Contraindicated if faecal impaction or bowel obstruction suspected.
Use cautiously in irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease.
notes: Works by increasing stool bulk and water content.
Takes several days to become effective (up to 2-3 weeks for full benefit).
Require adequate fluid intake (at least 6-8 glasses daily).
Patient must take with sufficient water (at least 150 mL per sachet) to avoid choking or intestinal obstruction.
Gradual introduction reduces bloating; start with half-dose and increase over 1-2 weeks.

regimens.label: 2nd choice: Add stool softener if osmotic/bulk-forming alone insufficient

components.dose: 100 mg once to three times daily

notes: Anionic surfactant; softens stool by increasing water penetration.
Often used in combination with osmotic laxatives.
Effect within 1-3 days.
Particularly useful when hard stools are the predominant problem.

regimens.label: 3rd choice: Stimulant laxative if other measures insufficient (short-term use only)

components.dose: 7.5-15 mg once daily at bedtime; increase if necessary to max 30 mg daily
components.duration: short-term use only; review after 2-4 weeks and plan to discontinue

restrictions: Avoid long-term use due to risk of melanosis coli and colonic motor dysfunction.
Contraindicated in inflammatory bowel disease or acute inflammatory conditions.
notes: Increases colonic motility; effect in 8-12 hours.
Abdominal cramping common; warn patient.
Not first-line for routine constipation but useful for opioid-induced constipation.
Tolerance can develop with long-term use.

regimens.label: 3rd choice: Alternative stimulant — bisacodyl

components.duration: short-term use only; review after 2-4 weeks and plan to discontinue
short-term use only; review after 2-4 weeks and plan to discontinue

restrictions: Avoid long-term use due to risk of colonic motor dysfunction.
notes: Stimulant action; tablets work in 6-12 hours, suppository in 15-60 minutes.
Suppository route useful for rapid effect or if patient unable to take oral medication.
Can cause abdominal cramping.

specialConsiderations.title: Opioid-induced constipation
items: Stimulant laxatives (e.g. senna) preferred as first-line over osmotic agents.
Consider co-prescribing a laxative when starting opioids; do not wait for constipation to develop.
May require higher doses or combination therapy due to opioid effect.
Ensure adequate fluid and fibre intake alongside laxatives.

specialConsiderations.title: Older adults
items: Constipation common in older age; reassure and manage expectation.
Review medications for constipating agents (opioids, anticholinergics, calcium antagonists).
Ensure adequate hydration and mobility if possible.
Osmotic laxatives (lactulose, macrogol) preferred as first-line.
Stimulant laxatives only if osmotic agents alone insufficient; avoid long-term use.
Monitor for faecal impaction risk, especially if immobile or receiving strong opioids.

specialConsiderations.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
items: Constipation common; reassure and manage with lifestyle measures first.
Osmotic laxatives (lactulose, macrogol) safe in pregnancy; preferred first-line.
Bulk-forming laxatives safe if adequate fluid intake.
Avoid stimulant laxatives in pregnancy unless essential (senna relatively safe if needed).
All laxatives pass minimal amounts into breast milk; safe during breastfeeding.

specialConsiderations.title: Chronic or refractory constipation
items: After 2-4 weeks with no improvement, refer to secondary care for further assessment.
Consider colorectal specialist assessment if red-flag symptoms or suspected organic cause.
Secondary care may offer specialist agents (e.g. prucalopride) or assessment for underlying motility disorder.
